components.text: The proposed external reason must be a coherent necessary being rather than another unexplained existent.
Whether the proposed external reason can coherently be a necessary being.
Whether the totality requires any external sufficient reason at all.
A necessary conclusion may be conditional on an empirically discovered contingent being rather than resting on an analytic existential premise.
Whether an empirical premise can support a necessary conditional inference without itself being analytic.
The asserted necessary being appears to require treating its existence as analytically included in its essence.
The external sufficient reason must be characterized without illegitimately making existence a predicate of a named being.
Whether the claimed necessary being avoids an ontological inference that treats existence as a predicate.
Whether contingent totality requires an external sufficient reason.
God's existence is inferred from experience before essence-existence identity is argued, so existence is not inserted into an a priori definition.
Knowledge of the relevant being begins from experience rather than an analytic existential proposition.
Whether Copleston's argument defines God into existence or begins from experience.
Whether necessary existence must be known through an analytic proposition.
Explanatory practices concerning particular objects do not by themselves license a causal or sufficient-reason demand for their totality.
Whether causal explanation of particulars licenses a cause or sufficient reason for their totality.
Whether experience of contingency entails a necessary being.
Whether the inferred being has identical essence and existence.
The same private experiential confidence supports incompatible supernatural objects, so testimonial phenomenology does not discriminate God.
Whether private mystical conviction discriminates God from incompatible reported objects.
Wholesome transformation caused by an experience does not verify that the experience has an object outside the subject.
Whether profound beneficial transformation verifies a reality external to the experiencer.
Whether the phenomenology itself is better explained by an objective transcendent cause.
Beneficial influence from a loved figure does not establish that the figure exists, because fictional figures can produce the same effect.
Whether beneficial influence from a loved apparent object establishes that object's existence.
Whether mystical phenomenology independently warrants an objective cause.
The objective-cause inference from mystical phenomenology requires independent discrimination from subjective explanations.
Whether mystical awareness is better explained by an objective transcendent cause.
Goodness is not simply identical with God; it reflects and proceeds from God, and that interpretation depends on independently recognizing God.
Whether Copleston is merely defining God as the sum or system of goodness.
The claim that genuine goodness reflects and proceeds from God requires support beyond prior recognition of God.
Whether goodness reflects and proceeds from an independently recognized divine source.
Feeling alone cannot supply a correctness standard when agents feel differently about conduct, including atrocious conduct.
Whether feeling alone supplies a standard for condemning morally atrocious conduct.
Historically changing perceptions of duty challenge the asserted absoluteness and universal recognition of moral law.
Whether moral law is absolute given substantial historical change in perceived duties.
The possibility of criticizing accepted codes distinguishes variable moral beliefs from an objective ideal standard.
An objective ideal order supplies a correctness standard beyond the feelings or conventions of a group.
Whether changing accepted codes defeats an objective ideal moral order.
Whether moral criticism requires a standard beyond feeling and accepted practice.
The experienced sense of ought can be explained through imagined disapproval, custom, taboo, environment, and education rather than God.
A naturalistic causal account is offered for moral obligation, opposing the claim that a transcendent lawgiver best explains it.
Whether the sense of obligation requires a transcendent author rather than natural social formation.
Whether objective criticism and obligatory character require a divine foundation.
